subject: Climate & Environment
title: Indigenous Peoples and Forest Loss
description: A quick, practical guide to Indigenous Peoples and Forest Loss.

hook.text: About 370 million Indigenous people depend on forests for food, shelter, and identity.

buildup.text: Indigenous lands make up 22% of the world's surface but hold 80% of remaining biodiversity.

discovery.text: Studies show deforestation rates are far lower on land managed by Indigenous communities.

twist.text: Despite this, land rights are often ignored. Loggers and ranchers push people off their land.

climax.text: Securing Indigenous land rights may be the single most effective conservation strategy.

punchline.text: The best forest guardians are the ones who lived there first.

quiz.question: How much of the world's remaining biodiversity is on Indigenous lands?

details.summary: Indigenous peoples manage or hold tenure over approximately 36 percent of the world's remaining intact forests. Studies consistently show that indigenous-managed lands experience lower deforestation rates than surrounding areas, including government-designated protected areas.
details.whyItMatters: Indigenous forest stewardship is among the most effective and cost-efficient conservation strategies. Securing indigenous land rights directly protects forests and climate.
takeaways: Indigenous lands lose forest at a fraction of the rate of surrounding areas
Many indigenous communities face violence and displacement from land grabs
Recognizing indigenous tenure is cheaper than other protection methods

faq.question: Why are indigenous-managed forests better protected?
faq.answer: Indigenous communities have deep ecological knowledge, economic dependence on forest health, and social systems that regulate resource use. Their continuous presence deters illegal logging and land grabs more effectively than remote government patrols.

faq.question: How are indigenous land rights threatened?
faq.answer: Land grabs by ranchers, miners, and agribusiness, often with government complicity, are the main threats. Weakening of environmental protections, reduced funding for enforcement, and violence against indigenous leaders continue in many countries.
